venues.name: Six Senses Zil Pasyon
venues.area: Félicité (private island, near La Digue; boat or helicopter transfer)
venues.note: Thirty pool villas scattered across a granite-boulder island, the most complete expression of Six Senses wellness in the Indian Ocean, with a spa carved into the rocks.
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler, Triple Crown Award; Hot List on opening
Tatler Spa Guide Award

venues.name: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles
venues.area: Mahé (Petite Anse / Baie Lazare, southwest coast)
venues.note: The benchmark for polished, family-capable luxury on the main island, treehouse-style villas terraced down a jungle hillside to a private horseshoe bay.
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide, Four Star
MICHELIN Guide hotel selection (a hotel listing, not a dining star)

venues.name: Anantara Maia Seychelles Villas
venues.note: Thirty villas on a private peninsula wrapped in thirty acres of jungle, a butler-for-every-villa, all-inclusive sanctuary designed by Bill Bensley.
credentials: Anantara / Minor Hotels flagship, award-winning gardens and spa
Recognised across the luxury travel trade for its all-villa, butler-led model

venues.name: Raffles Seychelles
venues.area: Praslin (Anse Volbert / Baie Sainte Anne, north coast)
venues.note: Praslin's grande dame, 86 hillside pool villas above the beach, with the storied Raffles service and easy reach of the Vallée de Mai and La Digue.
credentials: World Travel Awards, Indian Ocean's Leading Luxury Resort and Leading Honeymoon Resort (multiple years)
Forbes Travel Guide-recognised; Condé Nast Traveller Hot List (opening)

venues.name: Constance Ephélia
venues.area: Mahé (Port Launay, northwest coast, on the Port Launay Marine Park)
venues.note: A sprawling estate across two beaches and 120 hectares, home to one of the largest spas in the Indian Ocean, the most versatile big resort on Mahé.
credentials: Constance Hotels flagship, Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards nominee
Award-winning Spa de Constance (one of the region's largest)

venues.name: Mango House Seychelles, LXR Hotels & Resorts
venues.area: Mahé (Anse aux Poules Bleues, Baie Lazare, southwest coast)
venues.note: The former home of Italian photographer Gian Paolo Barbieri reborn as a design-led boutique retreat, the most stylish, character-rich address on Mahé.
credentials: Hilton's LXR Hotels & Resorts, the group's Seychelles property
MICHELIN Guide hotel selection (a hotel listing, not a dining star)

venues.name: '20 Degrees Sud'
venues.note: Anantara Maia's signature table, a hilltop or intimate wine-cellar setting for Creole-Mediterranean cooking and hard-to-find wines, the most refined dining experience on the main island.
credentials: Anantara Maia's award-winning signature restaurant

venues.name: ZEZ
venues.area: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles, Mahé (Petite Anse)
venues.note: Four Seasons' hilltop restaurant, high above the bay, an inventive sharing menu at night with one of the best ocean views on the island.
credentials: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles' signature dinner venue (Forbes Four-Star resort)

venues.name: Kannel
venues.area: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles, Mahé (Petite Anse)
venues.note: Beachside all-day dining at the Four Seasons, marrying Mediterranean flavours with Creole tradition, ceviches and salads by day, seafood and pasta by night.
credentials: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles restaurant (Forbes Four-Star resort)

venues.name: Marie Antoinette
venues.area: Mahé (Serret Road, St Louis, above Victoria)
venues.note: The islands' most storied Creole table, a set feast of parrotfish, tuna, aubergine fritters and chicken curry served in a colonial planter's house since 1972.
credentials: One of the oldest and most celebrated Creole restaurants in the Seychelles (est. 1972); a long-standing press and guidebook fixture

venues.name: Del Place
venues.note: A seafront Creole seafood house on the quiet west coast, tables almost in the water, with sunsets over the neighbouring islands.
credentials: A long-running west-coast Creole seafood institution, widely recommended in Seychelles dining guides

venues.name: La Plage
venues.note: Feet-in-the-sand Italian-Creole cooking on the island's most famous beach, the archetypal Beau Vallon sundowner-and-dinner.
credentials: A landmark restaurant on Beau Vallon, the Seychelles' best-known beach, and a fixture of local dining guides

venues.name: Vallée de Mai, the primeval palm forest
venues.note: A UNESCO-listed valley where you walk through a forest almost unchanged since prehistory, the world's last great stand of the coco de mer palm, whose 20kg double-lobed nut is the largest seed on Earth and whose suggestive shape once fed legends that this was the original Garden of Eden. Go early with a naturalist guide, listen for the rare Seychelles black parrot found nowhere else, and let the cathedral hush of the primeval forest do the rest.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Vallée de Mai Nature Reserve (inscribed 1983)

venues.name: Anse Source d'Argent, the granite-boulder beach
venues.note: The most photographed beach in the world, a string of shallow, glass-clear coves screened by sculpted pink granite boulders 750 million years old, reached on foot through the L'Union Estate coconut plantation. Come at low tide in the soft late-afternoon light, ideally by bicycle from the jetty, for the barefoot, camera-in-hand honeymoon picture the Seychelles is famous for.

venues.name: Anse Lazio, Praslin's crescent
venues.note: A wide arc of powder sand framed by takamaka trees and warm granite, repeatedly ranked among the best beaches on the planet by CNN and TripAdvisor and calm enough for a long swim off the rocks at either end. Arrive mid-morning before the day-trippers, take lunch at one of the two beach restaurants, and treat the whole afternoon as the definition of unhurried.
credentials: Repeatedly ranked among the world's best beaches (TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice; CNN)

venues.name: Anse Georgette, the hidden gem
venues.note: A perfect, near-empty white bay inside the grounds of Constance Lémuria, access is free but must be arranged in advance if you are not a resort guest, which keeps the crowds away and the sand pristine. For couples chasing the barefoot-billionaire seclusion the Seychelles promises, this is the quiet counterpoint to busier Anse Lazio.
credentials: Ranked among the world's 50 best beaches (World's 50 Beaches)

venues.name: Curieuse Island giant-tortoise day trip
venues.note: A twenty-minute boat hop lands you on a russet-earthed island where some 300 free-roaming Aldabra giant tortoises graze among the mangroves and a boardwalk threads a rare coco-de-mer-and-mangrove landscape. Pair it with a Creole barbecue lunch on the sand and a snorkel stop; a private charter turns a good excursion into an unhurried, uncrowded one.

venues.name: St Pierre islet snorkelling
venues.note: A picture-book cluster of granite boulders crowned with palms, ringed by some of Praslin's clearest water and busiest reef fish, the classic snorkel stop on a Curieuse day trip. Charter a private boat to arrive before the group excursions and you may have the whole jewel-like islet to yourselves.

venues.name: Cousin Island seabird sanctuary
venues.note: A strictly protected conservation island reached only on a guided landing, where thousands of nesting seabirds, hawksbill turtles and the once-vanishing Seychelles magpie-robin have been brought back from the brink. Visitor numbers are capped and mornings only, a rare, deeply intimate wildlife encounter for travellers who value pristine nature over crowds.

venues.name: Aride Island, the northernmost bird island
venues.note: The Seychelles' most important seabird island, over a million birds and the largest colonies of some species on Earth, landing on a wild, roadless nature reserve open only a few days a week and closed in the roughest season. A private boat and a calm-sea day make it one of the archipelago's great, little-seen natural spectacles.

venues.name: Beau Vallon beach
venues.note: Mahé's long, easy, palm-backed north-coast bay, the most reliable place on the island for a proper year-round swim, with sunset paddleboarding, a Wednesday-evening bazaar and casual Creole grills a short stroll away. An unfussy home base for a family who want the sea on the doorstep rather than a trek to a wild cove.

venues.name: Anse Intendance, the wild south beach
venues.note: A broad, undeveloped stretch of white sand and rolling surf in Mahé's untamed south, framed by granite headlands and backed only by takamaka trees, the beach beside Banyan Tree and among the most dramatic on the island. Magnificent for a long walk and a photograph; the currents are strong when the trade winds blow, so it's for watching the ocean's power more than swimming.

venues.name: Anse Takamaka
venues.note: A gently curving south-coast bay of pale sand and clear water named for the shade trees that line it, famous for its sunsets and, on calm days, its snorkelling. Chez Batista on the sand serves grilled fish with your toes in the sand, the essence of a slow Mahé afternoon.

venues.name: Petite Anse
venues.note: A flawless, sheltered cove within the Four Seasons estate but open to the public, reached down a short forest path, with soft powdery sand and gentle water that make it one of the south coast's most swimmable beaches. A discreet, resort-tended stretch of sand for couples who want beauty without the trek.

venues.name: Anse Soleil & Anse Soleil beach
venues.note: A tiny, boulder-flanked south-western cove at the end of a steep road, with excellent snorkelling straight off the sand and a beloved barefoot Creole café above it. Small, sheltered and gloriously out of the way, the reward for a driver who knows the back lanes of Baie Lazare.

venues.name: Sir Selwyn Selwyn-Clarke Market
venues.note: The beating heart of the tiny capital since 1840, a covered market piled with tropical fruit, vanilla pods, cinnamon bark, chilli and the morning's reef catch, best at 8am when the fishmongers set out. A short, sensory, grounding stop between beaches, and the place to understand how Creole, African, Indian and French flavours met on these islands.

venues.name: The Clock Tower (Little Big Ben)
venues.note: The silver Victorian clock tower erected in 1903 at the crossroads of the capital, modelled on a London original and the postcard symbol of Victoria, one of the smallest capital cities in the world. A five-minute stroll takes in the tower, the market and the Hindu temple; a gentle way to feel the island's colonial layer.

venues.name: Arul Mihu Navasakthi Vinayagar Temple
venues.note: The only Hindu temple in the Seychelles, a vividly painted gopuram on Quincy Street, built in 1992 and dedicated to Lord Vinayagar (Ganesha), serving the island's small Tamil-descended community. A moment of the familiar for Indian travellers, and a reminder of how far the diaspora and its gods have travelled across the Indian Ocean.

venues.name: Seychelles National Botanical Gardens
venues.note: A century-old garden on the edge of the capital with 200-plus species, coco de mer palms, a spice grove, orchids, a colony of fruit bats and a paddock of feedable Aldabra giant tortoises. A cool, shaded, easy hour for grandparents and children alike, a short drive from the harbour.

venues.name: The National Museum of History
venues.note: The capital's museum of Seychelles history housed in a restored colonial building, the Stone of Possession that claimed the islands for France, pirate lore, and the Creole story of settlement, slavery and independence. A short, well-curated context stop for travellers who like to understand a place before they lie on its beaches.

venues.name: Morne Seychellois National Park
venues.note: The mist-forested spine of Mahé, a protected mountain wilderness of cloud forest, endemic pitcher plants and hidden trails climbing to the island's 905m high point. The wild green heart behind the beaches, best explored on foot with a guide who can read the endemic flora.

venues.name: The Copolia Trail
venues.note: The island's most rewarding short hike, an hour through shaded palm forest to a bald granite dome at nearly 500m, with an eagle's-eye sweep over Victoria, the Sainte Anne islands and, on a clear day, Praslin and La Digue. Manageable for most fitness levels and the single best view on Mahé for the effort.

venues.name: Morne Blanc & the Tea Factory
venues.note: A steep, short nature trail climbing to a sheer-drop lookout over Mahé's west coast, beginning near the little hillside tea plantation that has grown Seychelles tea since 1962. Combine the walk with a stop at the tea factory shop for vanilla and citronella teas, a fragrant, cool interlude high above the sea.

venues.name: Sauzier Waterfall (Port Launay)
venues.note: A ten-minute walk through a private garden brings you to a jungle waterfall tumbling into a cool freshwater pool you can swim in, a rare, refreshing counterpoint to the salt and the sun. Easy enough for children, quiet enough for couples, and a lovely hidden gem near the west-coast beaches.

venues.name: Mission Lodge (Venn's Town) viewpoint
venues.note: The ruins of a 19th-century school for the children of freed slaves, high on the Sans Souci road, with a hilltop gazebo built for Queen Elizabeth II's 1972 visit that frames a sweeping view of Mahé's forested west. A poignant piece of history and one of the island's most cinematic viewpoints in a single easy stop.

venues.name: Takamaka Rum Distillery, La Plaine St André
venues.note: The island's craft rum distillery set in a restored 1792 plantation house, with guided tours, tastings, resident giant tortoises named Taka and Maka, a garden restaurant and Friday-night cocktails and live music. A relaxed, characterful half-day and the obvious place to taste, and take home, the Seychelles' signature spirit.

venues.name: Domaine de Val des Prés craft village
venues.note: A cluster of traditional wooden Creole houses restored as artisan workshops, model boat-builders, jewellers, potters and a plantation-house restaurant serving classic island cooking. The most tangible taste of old Creole life and craft on Mahé, and a good place to buy something genuinely local.

venues.name: Baie Lazare & the south-western coves
venues.note: A sleepy fishing village that gives its name to the loveliest tangle of coves in Mahé's south-west, the gateway to Anse Soleil, Petite Anse and Anse Gaulette, with a hilltop church and Creole eateries. The area to base a day of unhurried cove-hopping with a private driver.

venues.name: Anse Royale
venues.note: A long, reef-protected east-coast beach with calm, shallow water ideal for family swimming and snorkelling at the little offshore island, backed by a friendly village and casual takeaways. An easygoing, local-feeling stretch that balances Mahé's wilder south beaches.

venues.name: Eden Island
venues.note: A modern marina-and-residence development off Victoria with waterfront restaurants, a small mall and the archipelago's main yacht berths, the practical launch point for many private charters and a pleasant evening stroll and dinner by the boats. Useful and comfortable rather than wild, and where a chartered yacht will likely meet you.

venues.name: Grand Anse & Petite Anse, La Digue
venues.note: La Digue's dramatic south-east coast, Grand Anse a wide, powerful surf beach and, over the headland on foot, the quieter, more sheltered Petite Anse and Anse Cocos. A beautiful, breezy bicycle-and-walking loop through the island's wild side, best when the sea is calm from October to April.

venues.name: The ox-cart & bicycle island life of La Digue
venues.note: An island with almost no cars, where the traditional way to travel is by bicycle or ox-cart along sandy lanes past pastel Creole houses and vanilla plantations. Renting a good bike for the day is the whole point of La Digue, the slowest, most charming pace in the Seychelles.

venues.name: Nid d'Aigle viewpoint
venues.note: The 'Eagle's Nest', La Digue's 333m high point, reached by a steep track (best by hired local transport for part of the way, then on foot) to a panorama over the island's granite peaks and the turquoise channel to Praslin. The reward for the effort is the finest view in the inner islands.

venues.name: L'Union Estate, La Digue
venues.note: The historic coconut-and-vanilla plantation you pass through to reach Anse Source d'Argent, an old copra mill turned by an ox, a colonial plantation house, a vanilla plot and a pen of giant tortoises. A living slice of 19th-century island life that adds depth to the world's most photographed beach.

venues.name: Sainte Anne Marine National Park
venues.note: The Indian Ocean's first marine park, six islands just off Victoria, with over 150 species in the clear channels, easy snorkelling among hawksbill turtles and reef fish, and glass-bottom-boat trips for those who prefer to stay dry. A gentle, family-friendly introduction to the underwater Seychelles, minutes from the capital.

venues.name: Diving the inner islands
venues.note: Warm, clear water over granite drop-offs, wrecks and reefs alive with turtles, rays, whale sharks in season and the occasional reef shark, with reputable dive centres on Mahé and Praslin catering to first dives and log-book veterans alike. The archipelago's granite topography makes for some of the Indian Ocean's most atmospheric diving.

venues.name: Whale-shark encounters (seasonal)
venues.note: Between roughly August and October the world's largest fish gathers off Mahé's coast, and licensed operators run respectful swim-alongside snorkel trips to meet these gentle giants. A once-in-a-lifetime, strictly seasonal experience, worth timing a trip around for wildlife-minded travellers.

venues.name: Deep-sea game fishing
venues.note: The drop-offs and banks off the Seychelles hold sailfish, marlin, wahoo, dogtooth tuna and giant trevally, some of the Indian Ocean's finest big-game and fly-fishing, from half-day trolls to serious blue-water charters. A private boat with a seasoned skipper turns it into a bespoke day at sea.

venues.name: Fond Ferdinand Nature Reserve
venues.note: A less-visited, guided alternative to the Vallée de Mai, a steep-sided reserve with an even larger stand of coco de mer palms and, from its ridge, a rare panoramic view over Praslin and out to the neighbouring islands. Quieter and more strenuous, it rewards travellers who want the coco de mer forest with fewer people.

venues.name: Côte d'Or (Anse Volbert)
venues.note: Praslin's long, calm, palm-lined main beach, safe for swimming, dotted with beach restaurants and dive shops, and the departure point for boats to Curieuse, St Pierre and the bird islands. The convenient, easygoing base for a Praslin stay, with plenty for families.

venues.name: Creole cuisine & a spice-trail lunch
venues.note: Seychellois cooking is a fragrant crossroads, grilled bourgeois and job-fish, octopus curry, coconut and breadfruit, tamarind and chilli, and Indian palates find the spicing gloriously familiar, with good vegetarian and Indian options at the larger resorts. A long lunch at a beachside Creole table is as much a highlight here as any view.

venues.name: Katiolo
venues.area: Mahé (Anse Faure, east coast, near the airport)
venues.note: The Seychelles' oldest and most iconic nightclub, an open-air dancefloor by the sea, and about as close as the islands get to a genuine late night out.
credentials: The Seychelles' longest-running and best-known nightclub, the only beachside disco in the country

venues.name: Boardwalk Bar & Grill
venues.note: The marina-side gathering point on Eden Island, waterfront tables, live music and a late bar, the most reliable evening scene outside the resorts.
credentials: The marquee bar-and-grill on Eden Island, the Seychelles' upmarket marina development

venues.name: Boat House
venues.note: A Beau Vallon institution pairing a Creole buffet with a lively bar and live music, the beach's social anchor after dark.
credentials: A long-established Beau Vallon dining-and-bar landmark
